props.title: The Long Hot Summer
props.initialSlug: Southern romance sizzles amid family power plays

sections.content: The Long Hot Summer sizzles with sexual tension and Southern Gothic atmosphere, marking a pivotal moment in Paul Newman's rise to stardom. The film adapts multiple William Faulkner stories into a steamy Mississippi narrative that feels like Cat on a Hot Tin Roof (1958) meets Written on the Wind (1956). Newman and Joanne Woodward's electric chemistry (they married shortly after filming) drives this tale of a mysterious drifter who shakes up a wealthy family's dynamics. Director Martin Ritt captures the sultry Southern atmosphere with the same keen eye he'd later bring to Hud (1963) and Norma Rae (1979). movies.title: The Long Hot Summer
movies.slug: A charismatic drifter disrupts a wealthy Mississippi family's life when the patriarch takes him under his wing. Paul Newman and Joanne Woodward spark intense chemistry.

sections.content: Martin Ritt's direction established him as a master of Southern narratives, paving the way for films like To Kill a Mockingbird (1962) and In the Heat of the Night (1967). The film's exploration of class tensions and sexual repression influenced later Southern dramas like Sweet Bird of Youth (1962) and The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter (1968). Orson Welles delivers a powerhouse performance as the domineering patriarch Will Varner, channeling the same larger-than-life presence he brought to Touch of Evil (1958). SUBHEAD: Southern Gothic Cinema's Golden Age

The Long Hot Summer emerged during a remarkable period of Southern-themed Hollywood films that included A Streetcar Named Desire (1951) and Baby Doll (1956). These films dared to explore taboo subjects through the lens of Southern decay and repression. The film's success helped establish the careers of both Newman and Woodward, leading to their collaborations in Rachel, Rachel (1968) and The Glass Menagerie (1987). The sweaty, tension-filled atmosphere influenced later Southern Gothic works like The Night of the Hunter (1955) and Cape Fear (1962).
